newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany has high hopes for growth stock market.
newsitem.headline: Germany has high hopes for growth stock market.

text.p: The German bourse on Monday said it expected to attract as many as 15 firms this year to its forthcoming new market for growth stocks -- a system modelled on New York's NASDAQ.

In the first of a series of roadshow news conferences heralding the launch of the so-called New Market on March 10, bourse board member Reto Francioni said conditions were optimal for innovative firms to get involved in the project.
"The German market has a huge potential, especially among the small to mid-sized firms that form the backbone of its economy," Francioni said.
"We can offer a neutral platform for growth-rich companies -- mainly those with an international outlook -- who would like a higher degree of visibility," he added.

The New Market, whose launch was first announced last October, is the German bourse's latest bid to encourage investment in stocks and help innovative small firms, especially from the technology sector, to go public.

Companies will have to fulfil strict requirements on issue conditions and transparency to take part in the scheme, to help ease the risk factor attached to them, but will receive help and publicity from the bourse in return.
The scheme is aimed at firms which would find it difficult to drum up enough investor interest in the over-the-counter market to which their shares would normally be confined.

Despite its optimism about New Market's first year, the bourse conceded that the scheme will get off to a slow start. So far, only one company, the engineering firm Bertrandt AG, already a second-tier listed security, has committed itself to the project.
In the best-case scenario, a full German growth stock index -- which would have to involve at least 20 firms -- would not be possible for some 18 months after the launch.

"This is a project that will take some two, three, or even four years of observation," Francioni said, adding that he hoped the teething period would not be as long as NASDAQ's, whose boom came some 20 years after its launch.

The New Market scheme is partly a response to competitors such as NASDAQ, in which several German firms have expressed interest, and partly a bid to match risk-friendly investors with high-return shares.
"The demand is definitely there," Francioni said, noting that many individuals in Germany were seeking alternative investments as state pension reserves dwindle.

The exchange is putting its full weight behind the project, with roadshows planned in five German cities in the next two weeks and plans in place to link up with similar schemes in France, Belgium and the Netherlands.

Trading in the New Market stocks will initially take place only on the Frankfurt trading floor but will be extended to computerised dealings once the bourse introduces its new electronic trading system in 1998.
Each company will have its own "guardian" -- a role similar to a market maker and generally taken by the issuing bank -- who will guarantee to offer investors buy and sell prices on the stock.
The bourse said it would keep a close eye on the firms involved and would oust them from the scheme if they failed to meet the stringent transparency requirements.

The requirements include that at least 50 percent of the shares issued would come from a capital increase, that companies report results in German and English and according to international accounting standards, and hold regular conferences for the press and analysts.
"The New Market will play a model role, making risk easier to measure and assess," Francioni said. REUTER
